paras: Lucia and Renata are sisters, and they have not lived in the same place for fifteen years. Lucia stayed in Sao Paulo, thirty minutes from the street where they grew up. Renata moved to a town of nine thousand people, four hours away, in the countryside. They talk every Sunday, and about half of every call is the same argument about which of them made the better decision.

Renata's house is bigger and much cheaper than Lucia's apartment. It has a view of a valley, and the air is cleaner. It is also much quieter. Renata says it is the quietest place she knows, which she loves and Lucia finds slightly frightening. The nearest hospital is fifty minutes away. That is the sentence Lucia repeats every time she loses the argument.

Lucia's street is noisier, more crowded and more expensive, and the traffic is the worst part of her week. But her son walked to school on his own from the age of eleven, because the street is safe. She has three theaters within twenty minutes. And when their mother was ill, the ambulance took nine minutes. Lucia says the city is not more comfortable. It is more useful.

Neither of them is trying to convince the other any more. What changed is the question. For fifteen years they asked which place was better. Now they ask which one is better for the life you actually want, which is a harder question and a more honest one. Renata says the best thing about her town is that nothing happens. Lucia says that is the worst thing about it.
reading.source: A portrait written for this lesson, from a conversation that happens in a lot of families.

choices: To prove that the countryside is a better place to live than the city.
To show two honest lists side by side, and a question that is better than "which is better".
To explain how to choose a hospital near your house.

items.situation: Compare the two houses in one sentence, using than.
tips: Renata's house is bigger and much cheaper than Lucia's apartment.
Short adjectives grow a tail: bigger, cheaper. Never more bigger.

items.situation: Now compare the two streets, using a long adjective.
tips: Lucia's street is more crowded and more expensive than Renata's.
Long adjectives take more in front instead of a tail.

items.situation: Say what is at the top: the quietest, the worst, the best.
tips: The traffic is the worst part of her week.
Renata says it is the quietest place she knows.

items.situation: Say that two things are equal, and then that one is not.
tips: Option A is as safe as option B.
Option A is not as expensive as option B.

items.situation: Now compare two places you know, and give me one comparison of each kind.
tips: Tatuape is quieter than the center, and the center is more crowded.
One short adjective with a tail, one long adjective with more.

items.situation: Choose one of them and finish the sentence with because.
tips: I prefer Tatuape, because it is safer and I know everybody on my street.
Never stop at the choice. The because is the part that makes it a conversation.

listenings.text: People ask me which city was better, and I never know how to answer, because the honest answer is annoying. They were better at different things. The first one was cheaper, warmer and much friendlier. I knew the man at the bakery, I knew his dog, and I knew which day he made the good bread. It was also the more boring of the two, and by the third winter I could feel it. The second city is more expensive, colder and a lot less friendly. Nobody at my bakery knows my name and I doubt anybody ever will. But there is something on every night of the week, the trains work, and I am better at my job than I was, because the people around me are better at theirs. So which was better? The first one was a nicer life. The second one is a bigger one. I do not think you get both.

I want to argue with the word better, because it is doing too much work. Better at what? A car can be faster and less safe at the same time. A flat can be cheaper and further from everything. A job can pay more and cost you every Sunday. So when somebody asks me whether one thing is better than another, my first question back is always the same. Better for who, and better for which part of your life? It sounds like a way of avoiding the answer. It is the opposite. Once you finish the sentence, and I mean really finish it, cheaper than, closer to, quieter than, worse for my knees, the choice usually makes itself. And you stop arguing with people who simply want a different half of the same thing.
